question: A conference programme coordinator uploaded ten breakout-session proposals and asked Claude to summarise each one with a verdict against the published selection criteria. The reply is fluent and well organised. What should she do first?
options: A) Read each verdict carefully and decide whether it sounds reasonable to her on its own terms.
B) Forward the reply to the selection panel and invite its members to flag anything that looks wrong to them.
C) Ask Claude to shorten the summary so that the panel can work through the material more quickly.
D) Check the reply against what she asked for, confirming all ten proposals and every criterion appear.
correct_answers: D) Check the reply against what she asked for, confirming all ten proposals and every criterion appear.
explanations: Judging whether each verdict sounds reasonable tests plausibility, not coverage. It would not reveal that a proposal or a criterion had been left out altogether, which is the more likely failure with a batch of ten.
Handing an unchecked summary to the panel outsources the coordinator's own responsibility for the output and risks the panel treating a partial summary as the full field of proposals.
Shortening a summary that may already be missing proposals or criteria makes the gap harder to see, not easier. Length is a presentation choice and it is premature here.

Correct. A fluent reply can still be an incomplete one, and completeness is checked against the original request rather than against how the text reads. Confirming that all ten proposals and all the criteria are actually covered is the cheapest check available and it shapes everything she does next.
